claims.text: The retention of ductile toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the extent of grain-boundary elemental segregation.
Cooling rate during post-solidification heat treatment can control the governing grain-boundary microstructure.
Slower cooling promotes elemental segregation and coarsening of grain-boundary precipitates.
Coarse, irregular γ′ precipitates pin mobile grain boundaries and produce a serrated boundary morphology through Zener drag.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute local strain more uniformly than straight grain boundaries.
Serrated grain boundaries suppress or delay intergranular cracking.
Serrated grain boundaries increase tensile fracture strain and creep-rupture life relative to straight grain boundaries.
Faster cooling restricts grain-boundary diffusion and minimizes elemental segregation.
Faster-cooled material retains straighter grain boundaries and has lower ductility than slower-cooled material with serrated boundaries.
Slower cooling increases diffusion at grain boundaries and thereby produces local compositional fluctuations.
Increasing heat-treatment dwell time can substitute for reducing cooling rate to modulate segregation and precipitate coarsening.
The initial alloy may be a Cantor alloy with an equiaxed, predominantly single-phase FCC structure and minimal grain-boundary segregation produced by selective laser melting.
The mechanism should apply broadly to equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys that remain primarily FCC during conventional heat treatment.
The size of the toughness improvement depends on alloy chemistry and processing conditions.
Competing microstructural features not controlled by cooling rate may affect the observed mechanical response.
